first_impression.reaction: James's mum is Japanese-Australian and she's already asking about a yuino dinner, so I Googled it. The first line is exactly our situation: 'A Japanese wedding is a meeting of two families as much as two people.' No fluff, and it promised the day in order plus an Australian section at the end. Kept reading.

journey.quote: Parents are present at every stage, from the first formal exchange of gifts to the letter a bride reads aloud at the end of the reception.
journey.reaction: Calm, grown-up, no 'fairytale'. It tells me this is a family production. That's the conversation we're having at home.

journey.section: What a traditional Japanese wedding looks like today
journey.quote: Ask both families early which moments matter most to them, and build the day around those.
journey.reaction: Practical and honest. This is the thing that stops a family argument later.

journey.quote: Many couples now hold a Shinto ceremony for family, a chapel ceremony for friends and a long reception for everyone.
journey.reaction: Useful line, but it's a whole heading for one sentence and it repeats what I'd just read. Felt like filler.

journey.quote: Decide early who will host, and whether relatives who cannot travel will join by video.
journey.reaction: Exactly the question James's mum will ask. Grandparents in Japan joining by video is a real thing for us.

journey.section: 2. The Japanese wedding ceremony at a Shinto shrine
journey.quote: Ask the priest what guests may photograph and wear, and brief friends from overseas on quiet, respectful conduct during the rite.
journey.reaction: Good. Half our friends would be filming on their phones without this. Though again, who does the asking and the briefing? Us?

journey.section: 4. The bride's shiromuku, iro-uchikake and the groom's hakama
journey.quote: When you hire an uchikake, ask the stylist to explain its motifs, so you can share them with guests in the order of service.
journey.reaction: Lovely detail, and the kind of thing that makes it feel personal rather than costume. The museum history before it I skimmed.

journey.quote: Allow generous dressing time between them: a shiromuku takes far longer to put on than a gown.
journey.reaction: Insider stuff. I'd never have thought about that and it would wreck a timeline.

journey.quote: Build every outfit change into the run sheet, with a private dressing room close to the reception and a dresser on hand.
journey.reaction: Clear. Three outfit changes means someone has to own that run sheet, and I'd really like it not to be me at 11pm.

journey.quote: Ask a Japanese relative or friend what is expected in your circle: the custom is personal, and families have their own sense of what is fitting.
journey.reaction: Fair, and I appreciate it doesn't pretend there's one rule. My Australian family will need the goshugi explained to them, so I'd share this bit.

journey.section: 9. Speeches and the bride's letter to her parents
journey.quote: If your parents are not used to speaking in public, give them notice, and offer a translator if half the room will not follow the language.
journey.reaction: This is us exactly: two languages in one room. Really thoughtful.

journey.section: 11. Marrying in Japan as Australians: Travel and timing
journey.quote: Spring and autumn dates suit outdoor portraits and guests who are travelling far.
journey.reaction: Helpful with the heat and typhoon context. But for 70-odd guests, half flying in, there's nothing on where they'd stay or how my grandparents get from Narita or Kansai to Kyoto or Hakone. 'Couples who marry in Japan often choose Kyoto, Tokyo or Hakone' is one line and then links away.

journey.quote: Before you book, put these questions to the municipal office (the kuyakusho or shiyakusho) where you plan to marry, and to the Australian Embassy:
journey.reaction: The question list is genuinely good and specific. The shrine-versus-municipal-office registration question is the one I'd have missed. Still, legal is the bit I most want someone else to handle.

journey.quote: Many Japanese-Australian couples marry in Australia, with san-san-kudo in the ceremony, a change into kimono for the reception, kagami biraki for the toast and the bride's letter before the last speech.
journey.reaction: Realistically this could be us. It's short, though. I'd like a bit more on how a planner fits around a family who will want to lead half the day.

journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the parts your families lead, as your single point of contact.
journey.reaction: Best line on the page for me. 'Around the parts your families lead' is exactly what I wanted to hear, and 'single point of contact' answers who's accountable.

journey.quote: They work in your time zone and quote in AUD, the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Currency surprises and hidden costs, both addressed. Good.

journey.quote: The municipal office and the Embassy set the legal steps, and the shrine or chapel sets its own.
journey.reaction: Honest, and less of a door-slam than I expected. But I still don't know whether the advisor helps us with any of the paperwork or just schedules around it.

journey.section: Planning your Japanese wedding with us
journey.quote: To keep dreaming first, [read the free Wedded Wonderland magazine]
journey.reaction: 'Keep dreaming' is a touch soft for me after such a practical article, but it's not a hard sell, which I prefer.

unanswered_questions: Have you planned a Japanese or Japanese-Australian wedding before? Is there a real one with a venue and date I can look at?
If we married in Japan, where would 60 to 90 guests stay, and how would older relatives get from the airport to Kyoto or Hakone?
Who owns the run sheet with the outfit changes, dressers and ceremony times: you, us, or the venue?
Does the Wedded Advisor help with the municipal office and CNI paperwork in any way, even if we lodge it ourselves?
Can you arrange the shrine booking, kimono hire and dressers, or do we find those ourselves?
Can you organise a translator or bilingual MC for a two-language reception?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Japanese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Reads like clickbait; the article is better than its title. Noted only, I understand it's set and not must-fix.

would_share_with: James's mum (yuino, Shinto ceremony, kimono and the bride's letter sections)
My parents (goshugi and hikidemono, what to wear, and 'Bringing Japanese traditions home')

cta_reaction.quote: tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want, and a Wedded Advisor will start from there. Nothing is too early or too vague.
cta_reaction.why: Low pressure and 'nothing is too early' suits us at 14 months out. The written AUD fee and single point of contact are real pluses. But I want to see a real wedding where you've worked with a Japanese family first, so I'd read another post or two.

top_3_changes: Link to a real Japanese or Japanese-Australian wedding from your pages, with venue and date, so I can see you've done this before.
Add a few lines on what a Japan wedding means for travelling guests: where they stay, getting older relatives from the airport to Kyoto or Hakone, and who is on the ground on the day.

Say plainly who owns the run sheet (outfit changes, dressers, two ceremony times, translator) and what the Wedded Advisor does around the legal paperwork, and drop or merge the one-line 'Modern Japanese weddings' subheading.
